extracted.intended_audience: educated readers interested in culture, politics, education, and moral authority
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying standards the essay adduces for judging cultural, religious, literary, educational, and political authorities and institutions—what counts as genuine authority, good taste, and public example. The page argues for public recognition of a 'best self' or 'right reason' and criticises popular and institutional anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paramount authority of the best self / right reason
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be recognised a 'paramount authority of a commanding best self, or right reason' that stands above ordinary selves and custom, and that can serve as a sound centre of authority in literature, religion, and politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that without recognition of a best self/right reason we encourage a natural 'taste for the bathos' and lack a corrective to ordinary folly. Public institutions and leaders should promote this idea so individuals are drawn toward higher judgment rather than mere self-satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of literary (and other) organs measured by proximity to an ideal centre
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of newspapers, reviews, and other 'literary organs' should be judged 'relative to their being nearer a certain ideal centre of correct information, taste, and intelligence, or farther away from it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics should rank judgments on a scale of value according to closeness to that ideal centre; mere presence in the public sphere does not equal high authority. Example: Saturday Review may rank higher than smaller partisan papers because it is nearer that centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity and force do not establish doctrinal seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "That there are any further stricter tests to be applied to a doctrine, before it is pronounced important, never seems to occur to" those who judge doctrines by numbers and arms; '200,000 souls,--200,000 of the innumerable multitude ... to hold it, and 20,000 rifles to defend it' give the doctrine no seriousness for the best reason and spirit of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal or intellectual significance must be tested by quality of thought and relation to 'right reason', not by number of adherents or military/organisational strength. Anti-pattern: treating mass and force as proof of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of public platforms depends on intrinsic significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'fair and open field is not to be refused when hosts so mighty throw down wager of battle' is 'out of place unless he has, for the best reason and spirit of man, some significance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting a public platform or solemn heralding is inappropriate unless the speaker or doctrine has genuine intellectual significance; ceremonial publicity should not be accorded merely because of numbers or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governors and guides should set and exemplify high standards of right reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who govern or guide ought, 'by virtue of their superior means, power, and information, to set an example and to provide suggestions of right reason' instead of accommodating themselves to the natural tastes of those who elect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should use their elevated position to present corrective standards and examples; pandering and flattering the self-love of classes is an anti-pattern that sustains low standards of taste and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public action (State) should embody right reason to influence individual reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'the action of the State being the action of the collective nation... carries naturally great publicity, weight, and force of example with it', the State should try 'to put into the action of the State as much as possible of right reason' to help align individual reason with the best reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay defends using visible public institutions and policies as pedagogical examples that can 'come back to us with new force and authority' and thereby check the 'natural taste for the bathos.' It rejects the Quietist argument that reason will sort itself out without such embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public institutions should be planned and backed by competent authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Crown-patronage schools (Prussian example) show that schools established and endowed by the Sovereign 'to be under the direct control and management of him or those representing him' serve as types of what schools should be, benefiting from 'the best advice' and giving 'credit and authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design by informed authorities (experts, enlightened governors) confers example and standard-setting power. Anti-pattern: leaving schools to sectional private founders (e.g., 'Licensed Victuallers') whose character makes them unfit exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-supported education reforms as means to embody right reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete measures (from Humboldt's example) that enable the State to set educational standards: transference of school control to the State, obligatory State-examinations for schools and schoolmasters, and foundation of State universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural reforms are presented as effective ways the State can make visible, authoritative standards and help develop individual perfection—they are positive prescriptions rather than mere abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of flattering political rhetoric that comforts classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Political guides chosen by classes 'sing the praises of the Barbarians' or 'extol the earnest good sense' of the middle class—such flattering, comforting voices prevent classes from recognizing ignorance or prejudice and 'extinguish' prospects of inculcating higher taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative standard, political speech that primarily flatters and reassures rather than admonishes or raises standards should be treated as failing to promote public reason; it entrenches the 'taste for the bathos.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject doctrines that deny an ascertainable best self or reliance on providence to produce right reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Two criticised doctrines: (a) a form of 'Atheism' that maintains 'there is no such thing at all as a best self and a right reason ... nothing but an infinite number of ideas ... pretty equal in value'; (b) a 'Quietism' that asserts by leaving things to their natural operation (or Providence) society will arrive at right reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay treats both as inadequate; evaluative practice should not accept relativism (no higher centre) nor passive trust in providence as substitutes for active cultivation and institutional embodiment of right reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mechanism of social correction: the State's public action can make individuals reflect
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the State restrains eccentric or objectionable behaviour, such visible public restraint 'may yet fix clearly in their minds that, to the collective nation, these indulgences appear irrational and unallowable' and 'may contribute to bringing, with time, their individual reason into harmony with right reason.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an evaluative/strategic standard: measures that publicly mark behaviour as unacceptable can over time alter individual dispositions; so success should be judged not only by immediate coercion but by the long-run effect on individual reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural excellence requires balance between doing (Hebraism) and thinking (Hellenism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay posits two rival forces—energy driving practice (Hebraism) and intelligence driving thought (Hellenism)—and holds that human perfection demands a balance between them; overvaluing doing over thinking (or vice versa) is a defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cultural or educational projects, ask whether they cultivate both earnest practical virtue and the 'indomitable impulse to know'—a healthy culture will not be dominated by one at the expense of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders should deliver rebuke and example, not merely private by-play
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay notes that 'by-play' among the more intelligent leaders (private irony, tongue-in-cheek concessions) does not reach the mass of the governed; thus leaders must publicly rebuke and present higher standards so the governed may 'abate our self-love' and 'awaken in us a suspicion that our favourite prejudices may be ... nonsense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion for leadership and public writing: effectiveness includes the ability to reach the broader public with corrective, elevating messages rather than confining wisdom to private circles.
